nodes.name: OpenAI
nodes.jurisdiction: US company; applicable California and destination-market laws
nodes.description: Developer of frontier models with internal safety and release governance.
nodes.mechanism: Preparedness practices plus the May 2026 Frontier Governance Framework, with August operational updates.

powers.detail: Can obtain information from its own teams and systems.
No sovereign power to compel outside organizations.
Can investigate its own models, logs and deployment systems.
Can pause or change its own development and deployment.

gaps.detail: Corporate control does not confer public enforcement powers.
External scrutiny depends on evidence and model access granted to reviewers.

nodes.name: Anthropic
nodes.jurisdiction: US company; applicable California and destination-market laws
nodes.description: RSP v3 organizes risk thresholds, safety roadmaps and reports.
nodes.mechanism: Risk Reports every 3–6 months and external review; current commitments differ from earlier RSP versions.

powers.detail: Can obtain information from its own teams and systems.
No sovereign power to compel outside organizations.
Can investigate its own models, logs and deployment systems.
Can pause or change its own development and deployment.

gaps.detail: Corporate control does not confer public enforcement powers.
External scrutiny depends on evidence and model access granted to reviewers.

nodes.name: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
nodes.jurisdiction: United States federal
nodes.description: NIST’s current successor to the US AI Safety Institute.
nodes.mechanism: Voluntary standards and unclassified national-security evaluations; developer agreements expanded in May 2026.

powers.detail: Requests model access and information through collaboration.
These evaluation agreements confer no subpoena power.
Runs technical assessments of accessible models.
Can recommend mitigations, not universally prohibit model release.

gaps.detail: Evaluation mandate is not model licensing authority.
Nonpublic testing relies on negotiated developer access.

nodes.name: Model Evaluation & Threat Research
nodes.jurisdiction: US nonprofit; international voluntary partnerships
nodes.description: Independent nonprofit producing technical evidence on frontier capabilities and risks.
nodes.mechanism: Model evaluations, risk-report reviews and incident research; evidence can inform labs and regulators.

powers.detail: Requests model access, logs and information.
No legal disclosure-compulsion power.
Can technically investigate where access and evidence permit.
Recommends changes; cannot order a lab to implement them.

gaps.detail: Pilot participants could redact nonpublic information or exit silently.
Root-cause and remediation conclusions remain scientifically uncertain even with access.
Full incident investigations may take weeks or months.

nodes.name: Cloud and compute providers
nodes.jurisdiction: Global contracts and applicable local law; rights vary by provider
nodes.description: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud provide infrastructure on which labs and downstream services depend.
nodes.mechanism: Hosting, access controls and contractual suspension; AWS terms are the verified suspension example.

powers.detail: Can request customer cooperation and contractual information.
No public power to compel unrelated organizations.
Can investigate infrastructure within their access and contractual scope.
Can suspend their own services under applicable contract terms.

gaps.detail: Infrastructure visibility does not imply unrestricted model or customer-data access.
Suspension is contractual control, not sovereign model-remedy authority.

nodes.name: California Office of Emergency Services
nodes.jurisdiction: California, United States
nodes.description: Receives and reviews qualifying frontier-model incident reports under SB53.
nodes.mechanism: Mandatory incident intake and confidential internal-use risk-assessment summaries; referral to other authorities.

powers.detail: May seek clarification and cooperation.
Receives reports mandated by SB53; the Act does not establish a general Cal OES power to compel additional evidence. The Attorney General enforces reporting failures.
Reviews reports and can coordinate referrals; no general model-access or technical-investigation power is established by SB53.
SB53 gives no blanket Cal OES power to order model changes.

gaps.detail: Report review does not confer full model-access or general remediation powers.
Reports may need referral to AG or relevant public-safety authorities.

nodes.name: California Attorney General
nodes.jurisdiction: California, United States
nodes.description: Enforces SB53 compliance through civil actions.
nodes.mechanism: Civil penalties up to $1 million per violation for covered large developers; statutory whistleblower protections also apply.

powers.detail: Can request information concerning suspected noncompliance.
Evidence may be obtained through applicable legal process; SB53 is not unrestricted technical access.
Can investigate legal compliance; model analysis depends on technical evidence.
May bring civil-penalty actions. SB53 does not create a blanket model-release veto.

gaps.detail: Civil compliance enforcement differs from universal model-safety approval.
Legal investigation and technical root-cause evaluation are distinct functions.

nodes.name: Google DeepMind
nodes.jurisdiction: UK-based laboratory within US Google; applicable market laws
nodes.description: UK-based lab within Google, using a corporate frontier safety framework.
nodes.mechanism: FSF v3.1 adds tracked capability levels alongside critical thresholds and mitigations.

powers.detail: Can obtain information from its own teams and systems.
No sovereign power to compel outside organizations.
Can investigate its own models, logs and deployment systems.
Can pause or change its own development and deployment.

gaps.detail: Corporate control does not confer public enforcement powers.
External scrutiny depends on evidence and model access granted to reviewers.

nodes.name: UK AI Security Institute
nodes.jurisdiction: UK government research; developer access agreements and international partnerships
nodes.description: Tests frontier models before and after deployment and shares vulnerabilities with developers and public decision makers.
nodes.mechanism: Access agreements, technical evaluations and policy advice. Can stop its own testing, but cannot generally order a developer to withdraw a model.

powers.detail: Seeks developer information through cooperation and access arrangements.
No general regulatory power to compel developer disclosure.
Conducts technical testing and investigation using agreed access and its own research systems.
Can stop its own runs and secure its own environment; cannot generally compel an external model remedy.

gaps.detail: Independent technical findings do not create power to force a developer's disclosure or remedy.
Available model versions, safeguards and evaluation time depend on access arrangements.
The July incident illustrates uncertainty about how test behaviours generalise beyond evaluation settings.

nodes.name: UK National Cyber Security Centre
nodes.jurisdiction: UK cyber incident support and technical guidance
nodes.description: Helps organisations investigate and respond to cyber incidents and coordinates relevant government and international expertise.
nodes.mechanism: Incident support, technical indicators, security guidance and cooperation with affected organisations.

powers.detail: Requests information from affected organisations to support response.
Its incident-support role does not confer general regulatory disclosure powers.
Supports technical investigation with victim cooperation and access.
Can advise and assist mitigation; does not act as a general regulator ordering model remedies.

gaps.detail: Identifiable incident information is not shared with regulators without victim permission; reporting obligations remain with the victim.
Response effectiveness depends on receiving timely relevant evidence.

nodes.name: European Commission / AI Office
nodes.jurisdiction: EU market; GPAI providers, including foreign providers within AI Act scope
nodes.description: The European Commission, supported by the AI Office, oversees GPAI models and certain AI systems. This entry focuses on its GPAI enforcement powers, distinct from member-state responsibilities.
nodes.mechanism: AI Act Articles 91–93 and 101: information, technical access, evaluation, corrective measures and fines.

powers.detail: Request necessary compliance documentation and information under Article 91.
Providers must answer lawful requests; incorrect, incomplete or misleading information can attract fines.
Article 92 permits evaluations and required API or other technical access, including source code, subject to its conditions.
Article 93 permits mitigation, restricted availability, withdrawal or recall. Article 101 backs enforcement with fines.

gaps.detail: EU scope and premarket-research exclusions require analysis; no universal authority over every unreleased foreign model.
Additional evaluation capacity is planned for 2027; its announcement does not establish the adequacy of today's capacity.

nodes.name: EU GPAI systemic-risk obligations
nodes.jurisdiction: Providers of in-scope GPAI models with systemic risk in the EU
nodes.description: Binding duties require evaluation, systemic-risk mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity for qualifying GPAI models.
nodes.mechanism: Article 55; systemic-risk classification under Article 51. Models on the market before August 2025 have until August 2027.

powers.detail: The duties are not an actor. Commission Article 91 powers supply the associated information-request route.
The Commission can require relevant information under Article 91; the provider obligations alone are not a separate authority.
Article 55 requires provider evaluation. Independent Commission evaluation and access arise under Article 92.
Article 55 requires provider risk mitigation. Commission-ordered measures use the distinct Article 93 procedure.

gaps.detail: Systemic-risk classification, territorial scope, model vintage and research versus internal deployment affect coverage.
A legal evaluation duty does not settle whether an evaluation reliably measures every emerging risk.

nodes.name: EU Scientific Panel
nodes.jurisdiction: EU AI Act advisory and technical support
nodes.description: Independent specialists provide systemic-risk alerts, classification advice, evaluation expertise and market-surveillance support.
nodes.mechanism: Qualified alerts can lead to AI Office scrutiny; the Commission may obtain information or appoint experts for evaluation.

powers.detail: May request that the Commission obtain information needed for its statutory tasks.
No independent compulsory-disclosure power; Commission requests provide the legal route.
Experts can support or perform evaluations when appointed through the relevant procedure.
Alerts and advice inform Commission decisions; the panel cannot itself order a remedy.

gaps.detail: An expert alert must reach the authority able to obtain evidence and act.
Technical analysis depends on evidence provided through Commission and research access.

nodes.name: EU GPAI Code of Practice
nodes.jurisdiction: Voluntary compliance route for EU GPAI obligations
nodes.description: A practical route to demonstrate compliance with binding GPAI law. Non-signers must demonstrate other adequate means of compliance.
nodes.mechanism: Transparency, copyright, and safety/security chapters; an AI Office-chaired signatory taskforce supports implementation.

powers.detail: Signatories organise and submit compliance information through the Code's processes.
The Code has no independent compulsory-disclosure power; underlying AI Act duties remain binding.
Guides evaluations and risk-management practices; it does not itself authorise an external investigation.
Remedies depend on provider action and underlying Commission powers, not a separate Code regulator.

gaps.detail: Consistent implementation across signatories requires interpretation and oversight.
Do not confuse voluntary signature with voluntary compliance with the AI Act.

nodes.name: Cyberspace Administration of China
nodes.jurisdiction: Mainland China; public-facing generative services, including APIs
nodes.description: CAC and competent departments enforce public-service duties. Providers must address and report illegal content/activity; qualifying services undergo security assessment and algorithm filing. These are scoped service rules, not blanket oversight of all frontier research.
nodes.mechanism: Interim Measures, arts. 2, 14, 17, 19 and 21

powers.detail: May demand cooperation within statutory service scope.
Article 19 requires explanations of training data and algorithms plus necessary technical/data assistance.
Competent departments conduct supervision and inspections under article 19.
Article 21 allows correction orders and service suspension for refusal or serious cases.

gaps.detail: This instrument expressly excludes development/use not offered to mainland China's public.
A technical-assistance duty exists; practical effectiveness is not established here.

nodes.name: DeepSeek
nodes.jurisdiction: China-based developer; hosted services and separately distributed model weights
nodes.description: Develops models, provides hosted services and publishes technical reports/model cards. Corporate control covers its own development and hosted operations; distributed copies create a separate downstream governance problem.
nodes.mechanism: Internal model development, release decisions and hosted-service operation

powers.detail: Can request internal records through company management.
No public authority to compel external developers or users.
Can technically examine its own models and infrastructure.
Can change its own models/services; cannot reliably recall every independently hosted copy.

gaps.detail: External investigators need agreement or a valid statutory route.
Corporate control is bounded by its own systems and applicable contracts/law.

nodes.name: Korea Ministry of Science and ICT
nodes.jurisdiction: Republic of Korea; specified AI Basic Act violations
nodes.description: The AI Basic Act gives MSIT inspection and correction powers. Government announced at least one year of deferred routine fact-finding/penalties, with exceptional investigations for serious harm. Safety duties require all decree criteria, including training above 10^26 FLOPs.
nodes.mechanism: AI Basic Act article 40 and January 2026 implementation policy

powers.detail: Can request relevant information within the Act's scope.
Article 40 permits relevant document demands for specified suspected/reported violations.
Officials may inspect business sites and records; 2026 grace policy limits routine investigations.
May order cessation/correction of a violation; distinguish statutory power from current enforcement practice.

gaps.detail: The safety duty also requires state-of-the-art technology and broad/significant fundamental-rights risk.
An announced enforcement transition is not evidence of a staffing shortfall.

nodes.name: Singapore AI Safety Institute / Digital Trust Centre
nodes.jurisdiction: Singapore; DTC hosted at NTU with IMDA and NRF support
nodes.description: DTC serves as Singapore's AISI, developing evaluation/testing science and contributing to governance. It coordinates the research ecosystem and international scientific work.
nodes.mechanism: AI testing, research and international collaboration

powers.detail: Can invite company/research cooperation.
No standalone AISI disclosure mandate established.
Conducts evaluation and testing with available access.
Provides scientific input and tools rather than remedial orders.

gaps.detail: Distinguish the research institute from IMDA's separate sectoral regulatory functions.
Research access and technical methods condition investigation depth.

nodes.name: International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science
nodes.jurisdiction: Distributed network; location marks the current UK coordinating institute
nodes.description: Formerly the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. Connects national institutes and government offices through evaluation science and joint testing. UK AISI took the coordinating role after December 2025.
nodes.mechanism: Shared methods, research and joint evaluations

powers.detail: Members exchange information by agreement.
No supranational disclosure authority.
Member institutes conduct joint tests.
Findings do not become binding cross-border orders.

gaps.detail: Institutes retain separate mandates; membership does not transfer legal power.
Joint work depends on agreed model access and sharing terms.

nodes.name: OECD / G7 Hiroshima AI Process
nodes.jurisdiction: International; voluntary organizational participation
nodes.description: Provides a standard format for developer self-reporting against the G7 advanced-AI code. Version 2.0 simplifies reporting, including for smaller organizations.
nodes.mechanism: Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework

powers.detail: Requests self-reported alignment with the code.
Participation and disclosure remain voluntary.
Reporting supports scrutiny, not compulsory technical inspection.
Transparency and reputational pressure; no binding remedial order.

gaps.detail: Voluntary participation and self-reporting limit independent visibility.
The framework does not itself mandate developer remedies.

nodes.name: UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI
nodes.jurisdiction: Global; distributed scientific panel, Geneva dialogue venue shown
nodes.description: Synthesizes evidence on AI for global governance. Its preliminary assessment informed the July 2026 UN Dialogue. This is distinct from the International AI Safety Report process.
nodes.mechanism: Independent scientific assessment

powers.detail: Can draw on scientific contributions and public evidence.
No compulsory developer information power.
Scientific assessment rather than mandatory incident inspection.
Advises international deliberation; cannot order lab changes.

gaps.detail: Scientific synthesis cannot guarantee privileged model or incident-data access.
Evidence still needs translation into action by competent authorities.

nodes.name: ISO/IEC 42001
nodes.jurisdiction: International voluntary standard; no sovereign jurisdiction
nodes.description: Requirements for an AI management system in organisations developing or using AI.
nodes.mechanism: Management-system standard and assurance

powers.detail: Evidence collection can be part of implementing or assessing the management system.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.
Assesses organisational processes; not a sovereign technical investigation of a frontier model.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.

gaps.detail: A standard is not itself law. Additional contractual or legal incorporation needs separate analysis.
Management-system conformity does not prove absence of dangerous model capabilities.

nodes.name: African Union / Continental AI Strategy
nodes.jurisdiction: Africa; implementation through member states
nodes.description: Promotes Africa-centric, inclusive AI development and coordinated national governance. The strategy separates implementation of existing laws, identification of legal gaps and building institutional capability.
nodes.mechanism: Continental AI Strategy

powers.detail: Seeks member-state cooperation.
Strategy grants no direct power to demand lab information.
Strategic assessment, not a continental model inspection mandate.
Member-state institutions implement relevant legal remedies.

gaps.detail: Strategies require domestic legal implementation where existing laws are insufficient.
Skills, infrastructure and institutional capability are distinct development needs; country deficits differ.

nodes.name: European AI Board
nodes.jurisdiction: EU member-state cooperation under the AI Act
nodes.description: Member-state representatives promote coherent implementation and regulatory cooperation.
nodes.mechanism: Coordinates national perspectives; the AI Office consults the Board on GPAI evaluations.

powers.detail: Exchanges information and coordinates authorities within the AI Act framework.
No standalone power to compel a model developer's disclosure.
Consultation and coordination role; technical evaluations belong to competent actors.
Does not independently fine a provider or require model withdrawal.

gaps.detail: Common positions and referrals must translate into actions by the competent authorities.

nodes.name: EU national competent authorities
nodes.jurisdiction: Each EU member state; allocated AI-system and sectoral remits
nodes.status: Enforcement phased by obligation and national designation
nodes.description: A collective node for national market-surveillance and other competent authorities. It represents multiple authorities, not a single EU body.
nodes.mechanism: Investigations and corrective measures for applicable system-level rules; high-risk deadlines now December 2027 and August 2028.

powers.detail: Request system documentation within the authority's assigned national remit.
Compulsory information powers depend on the applicable provision and competent authority.
Investigate system compliance and risks under applicable market-surveillance powers.
Require corrective action or restrictions within remit; delayed duties cannot be enforced early.

gaps.detail: Current enforceability depends on the rule, country, designation and phased dates.
Country-level staffing and expertise must be checked individually; this map does not infer a uniform shortfall.
System-level evidence may require referral to the AI Office for model-level action.

nodes.name: France: INESIA
nodes.jurisdiction: France; national evaluation and security research
nodes.description: Connects ANSSI, Inria, LNE and PEReN under SGDSN/DGE coordination, without creating a new legal entity.
nodes.mechanism: Evaluates reliability and national-security risks and supports regulatory implementation.

powers.detail: May seek evidence and research partnerships through participating institutions.
No independent INESIA compulsory-disclosure mandate established by its creation.
Coordinates technical evaluation; access and powers depend on participating institutions and arrangements.
No independent INESIA power to order a frontier-model remedy established by these sources.

gaps.detail: A network's shared expertise should not be mistaken for a single enforcement mandate.
Evaluation requires relevant model and system access.

nodes.name: UK Information Commissioner's Office
nodes.jurisdiction: UK data protection; relevant processing of personal data
nodes.description: Investigates AI-related personal-data processing, with information, assessment and enforcement notices and financial penalties.
nodes.mechanism: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act oversight. A frontier incident must engage the data-protection remit.

powers.detail: May issue information notices in data-protection investigations.
Statutory notices require the relevant information or cooperation.
AI audits and assessment notices examine data-protection compliance; not unrestricted frontier-risk investigation.
Enforcement notices and penalties require compliance within data-protection scope.

gaps.detail: A model-capability incident without relevant personal-data processing may fall outside this mandate.
Cyber responders, model evaluators and privacy investigators hold different evidence and powers.

nodes.name: UK Ofcom
nodes.jurisdiction: UK-linked services and harms within the Online Safety Act
nodes.status: Enforcement active; chatbot scope must be checked
nodes.description: Enforces online-safety duties for covered services. Existing chatbot coverage and powers to expand it are distinct.
nodes.mechanism: Online Safety Act information gathering and enforcement; additional generative-AI duties require operative regulations.

powers.detail: Can seek information under online-safety powers for covered services.
Can use statutory information-gathering powers within its remit.
Investigates service systems and compliance; no general mandate to inspect every frontier model.
Can require compliance and use enforcement measures for applicable online-safety duties.

gaps.detail: Do not infer that enabling legislation has already brought every chatbot or model into scope.

nodes.name: UK Competition and Markets Authority
nodes.jurisdiction: UK competition and consumer-protection law
nodes.description: Can investigate consumer and competition harms involving AI. Businesses remain responsible for their AI agents' conduct.
nodes.mechanism: Direct enforcement, undertakings, remedies and penalties under applicable consumer and competition law.

powers.detail: May gather information for in-remit investigations.
Statutory investigation requirements can compel cooperation.
Can examine AI-related conduct and systems insofar as relevant to its legal remit.
Can impose in-remit remedies and penalties or accept undertakings; not universal model-safety orders.

gaps.detail: Consumer or competition jurisdiction is required; dangerous capability alone does not establish that trigger.

nodes.name: UK Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum
nodes.jurisdiction: UK cooperation among CMA, ICO, Ofcom and FCA
nodes.status: Voluntary forum; not a statutory entity
nodes.description: Coordinates expertise, foresight and approaches across digital regulators, which retain their own powers and accountability.
nodes.mechanism: Voluntary inter-regulator cooperation, shared research and coordinated policy work.

powers.detail: Supports information exchange and joint understanding among members.
No independent compulsory-disclosure power.
Coordinates research and expertise; member regulators conduct statutory investigations.
Cannot direct members or independently require company remedies.

gaps.detail: Shared analysis still requires each competent regulator to act under its own mandate.
A coordination forum cannot fill missing statutory jurisdiction by itself.

nodes.name: TC260 and CNCERT-CC
nodes.jurisdiction: China; influence through standards and sector regulators
nodes.description: Their AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 addresses open-model risks, CBRN misuse and loss of control. It informs China's technical standards and policy agenda; the framework itself is nonbinding.
nodes.mechanism: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0

powers.detail: Can seek technical contributions and evidence.
The framework creates no compulsory disclosure power.
Technical assessment and evaluation agenda.
Recommends mitigations; regulators need their own authority to order them.

gaps.detail: Guidance must be translated into an applicable legal or contractual duty.
Carnegie's 2025 analysis describes immature measurement science; no current staffing deficit is quantified.

nodes.name: Japan AI Safety Institute
nodes.jurisdiction: Japan; institute at IPA, separate from ministries' legal powers
nodes.description: Supports government with safety surveys, evaluation methods and guidelines; connects industry, academia and international institutes. July 2026 guidance expands evaluation perspectives for agents.
nodes.mechanism: Evaluation methods, guidance and scientific cooperation

powers.detail: Can request cooperation and research evidence.
No standalone compulsory disclosure power established in its remit.
Technical research and evaluation within available access.
Offers guidance, not independent remedial orders.

gaps.detail: Deep technical assessment depends on available models, environments and evidence.
AISI's technical remit does not transfer ministries' enforcement powers.

nodes.name: Korea AI Safety Institute
nodes.jurisdiction: Republic of Korea; technical institute, distinct from MSIT enforcement
nodes.description: Researches safety policy and technologies, evaluates systems and coordinates internationally. A July 2026 Canada–Korea MOU supports frontier evaluation and measurement.
nodes.mechanism: Technical evaluation, research and international MOUs

powers.detail: Can seek collaboration and technical information.
No standalone compulsory disclosure mandate established.
Evaluates AI and develops safety methods.
Technical recommendations; ministry powers are separate.

gaps.detail: Do not assign MSIT's AI Basic Act inspection/remedy powers to the institute.
Technical investigation requires relevant model/data access.

nodes.name: Canadian Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute
nodes.jurisdiction: Canada; ISED leads with NRC and CIFAR research capability
nodes.description: Studies advanced-system and synthetic-content risks through government-directed testing and funded research. Partners include Canadian institutes and international counterparts.
nodes.mechanism: Joint testing, investigator-led research and government advice

powers.detail: Seeks evidence through partnerships.
Its published remit establishes no standalone disclosure compulsion.
Conducts research and joint testing.
Provides guidance; other authorities enforce applicable laws.

gaps.detail: Frontier evaluation depends on research/model access.
Keep privacy, competition and sectoral enforcement separate from CAISI.

nodes.name: Australian AI Safety Institute
nodes.jurisdiction: Australia; Department of Industry, Science and Resources
nodes.description: Analyzes frontier models and supports existing regulators with technical evidence. It works with ASD, CSIRO and international partners, including through lab MOUs and joint tests.
nodes.mechanism: Technical testing and coordinated regulatory support

powers.detail: Seeks evidence through cooperation and lab MOUs.
No independent AISI compulsory disclosure power established.
Tests models and supports agency investigations technically.
Existing sector regulators, not AISI itself, apply their remedial powers.

gaps.detail: Evidence must reach the regulator whose law covers the harm.
MOU-based model access is different from compulsory inspection access.

nodes.name: IndiaAI Safety Institute
nodes.jurisdiction: India; MeitY / IndiaAI Mission hub-and-spoke network
nodes.description: Coordinates government, academia, startups and industry on safety research. Oversees Safe & Trusted AI projects within the IndiaAI Mission.
nodes.mechanism: Hub-and-spoke research, safety tools and project coordination

powers.detail: Can seek evidence and collaboration through the network.
No standalone general developer disclosure power established.
Supports risk assessment, testing and safety research.
Technical guidance and project oversight do not imply general remedial orders.

gaps.detail: Separate established AISI functions from governance mechanisms still proposed in guidelines.
Distributed expertise must be integrated through the hub-and-spoke structure.

nodes.name: UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance
nodes.jurisdiction: Global; first annual meeting in Geneva
nodes.description: Brings governments and stakeholders together to discuss international AI governance. The inaugural annual Dialogue took place 6–7 July 2026.
nodes.mechanism: Multistakeholder dialogue and policy coordination

powers.detail: Invites stakeholder contributions.
No direct developer disclosure compulsion.
Exchanges evidence; not a technical incident authority.
Discussion and recommendations do not create binding lab orders.

gaps.detail: Domestic and other applicable legal mechanisms are needed to enforce remedies.
Broad participation addresses representation but does not resolve all cross-border authority gaps.

nodes.name: UNESCO / AI Ethics and Readiness
nodes.jurisdiction: Global; national readiness assessments
nodes.description: Supports countries implementing its AI Ethics Recommendation. Readiness assessments examine legal, scientific, social, economic and technical conditions.
nodes.mechanism: Recommendation on AI Ethics and Readiness Assessment Methodology

powers.detail: Collects national information and stakeholder input.
No direct compulsory frontier-developer disclosure mandate.
Assesses national readiness rather than technically investigating incidents.
Recommends changes and supports implementation.

gaps.detail: Readiness work identifies country-specific capability needs.
Norms and capacity support require implementation by competent national institutions.

nodes.name: Alibaba / Qwen
nodes.jurisdiction: China-based Alibaba model team; hosted and independently deployed models
nodes.description: Alibaba's Qwen team develops language and multimodal models, with hosted chat and local deployment options. Its direct technical control is strongest inside its own model-development and service infrastructure.
nodes.mechanism: Model development, release decisions and hosted-service operation

powers.detail: Can obtain information through internal governance.
No general public power to compel outside disclosure.
Can examine its own models, development and service infrastructure.
Can change its own releases/services; independent deployments are outside direct operational control.

gaps.detail: Independent scrutiny needs public artifacts, agreement or a valid legal route.
Distributed deployment separates model-developer control from downstream system operation.

nodes.name: Meta
nodes.jurisdiction: US company; applicable California and destination-market laws
nodes.description: The Advanced AI Scaling Framework covers frontier deployments through open weights, APIs and closed products.
nodes.mechanism: Evaluations, release decisions and Safety & Preparedness Reports; loss-of-control risks added in 2026.

powers.detail: Can obtain information from its own teams and systems.
No sovereign power to compel outside organizations.
Can investigate its own models, logs and deployment systems.
Can pause or change its own development and deployment.

gaps.detail: Corporate control does not confer public enforcement powers.
External scrutiny depends on evidence and model access granted to reviewers.
Centralized recall and control diminish when model weights circulate downstream.

nodes.name: xAI / SpaceXAI
nodes.jurisdiction: US company; applicable state and destination-market laws
nodes.description: The public safety page uses SpaceXAI branding; the current framework identifies xAI LLC.
nodes.mechanism: June 2026 framework describes annual systemic risk assessment, lifecycle monitoring and release decisions.

powers.detail: Can obtain information from its own teams and systems.
No sovereign power to compel outside organizations.
Can investigate its own models, logs and deployment systems.
Can pause or change its own development and deployment.

gaps.detail: Corporate control does not confer public enforcement powers.
External scrutiny depends on evidence and model access granted to reviewers.

nodes.name: Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act
nodes.jurisdiction: California, United States
nodes.description: California’s 2026 frontier-model transparency and reporting regime.
nodes.mechanism: Models above 10^26 training operations; large-developer framework duties above $500m revenue. Qualifying reports: 15 days, or 24h for imminent serious injury to appropriate authority.

powers.detail: Defines required transparency and report contents.
Requires specified reports and framework disclosures; does not require all internal data.
Assigns report review and compliance enforcement, not universal direct model testing.
Enforceable framework compliance and civil penalties; no general premarket approval.

gaps.detail: Narrow incident categories leave many near-misses outside mandatory incident reporting.
Confidential reports are not public; absence of publication does not establish absence of reporting.

nodes.name: New York RAISE Act
nodes.jurisdiction: New York, United States; covered models operating/developed/deployed partly in state
nodes.description: Enacted frontier transparency framework with main duties scheduled for 1 January 2027.
nodes.mechanism: Future DFS reporting office; 72h incident reports and 24h imminent-injury route; AG penalties up to $1m first and $3m subsequent violations.

powers.detail: Future office can obtain reports within the enacted scheme.
Main reporting and publication duties begin 1 January 2027.
Future report review does not automatically confer unrestricted technical testing.
Future AG civil enforcement; not usable under this Act in the current tutorial.

gaps.detail: Main duties are not yet in force at the map cutoff.
Implementation and referral arrangements must support the future regime.

nodes.name: Federal Trade Commission
nodes.jurisdiction: United States federal
nodes.description: Consumer-protection and competition enforcement can reach AI-related conduct.
nodes.mechanism: Civil investigative demands, administrative proceedings and court injunctions within existing statutory jurisdiction.

powers.detail: Can seek voluntary information during inquiries.
Can issue compulsory investigative demands within an authorized investigation.
Can investigate AI-related practices; technical analysis requires relevant evidence.
May pursue binding orders or court remedies for violations within FTC jurisdiction.

gaps.detail: Not a universal frontier-model licensing or incident regulator.
Legal power to obtain evidence does not by itself supply every required AI specialty.

nodes.name: FBI, Department of Justice and courts
nodes.jurisdiction: United States federal
nodes.description: Investigates suspected criminal AI-enabled hacking and related offenses.
nodes.mechanism: Cyber investigations, lawful compulsory process and judicially authorized measures.

powers.detail: Receives incident reports and requests cooperation.
Compulsory evidence requires applicable legal process and predicates.
Cyber teams investigate suspected crimes, including technical evidence.
DOJ and courts can pursue remedies under criminal law; no blanket model-safety veto.

gaps.detail: A concerning model behavior alone does not establish a criminal predicate.
Cross-border evidence and victims require cooperation.

nodes.name: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency
nodes.jurisdiction: United States federal
nodes.description: Coordinates cyber defense and response, with particular authority over federal civilian systems.
nodes.mechanism: Voluntary private-sector incident assistance; federal binding directives; CIRCIA has a separate implementation track.

powers.detail: Requests incident and vulnerability information.
Federal-system authority differs from private-lab reporting; an effective CIRCIA final rule was not verified.
Can assist technical cyber response where scope and access permit.
Binding directives cover federal civilian systems, not every private AI model.

gaps.detail: No general private-lab model-safety enforcement mandate.
Sector and AI incident routes are separate; projected CIRCIA dates do not establish an active duty.

nodes.name: Bureau of Industry and Security
nodes.jurisdiction: US export law, with defined extraterritorial reach
nodes.description: Controls covered advanced-compute exports under US export jurisdiction.
nodes.mechanism: Export licensing and enforcement constrain upstream chip access; rules and destination conditions change.

powers.detail: Requests required information for license applications and compliance.
Can require export-related records within its statutory jurisdiction.
Investigates export compliance, not every model-safety incident.
Can restrict covered exports or enforce violations; no universal domestic model-release veto.

gaps.detail: Export-control scope differs from model-risk regulation.
Effectiveness depends on diversion verification and international cooperation.

nodes.name: Federal frontier cyber evaluation framework
nodes.jurisdiction: United States federal
nodes.description: EO14409 directs agencies to design classified frontier-cyber benchmarking and collaborative access.
nodes.mechanism: Voluntary access up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners; expressly no mandatory model licensing.

powers.detail: Invites developer cooperation and access.
This framework creates no compulsory developer disclosure scheme.
Agency experts can assess models available under agreed safeguards.
Section 3 creates no mandatory model preclearance or permitting power.

gaps.detail: Instructions bind agencies but do not make lab participation mandatory.
Classified and proprietary evidence require agreed access.
IAPS identifies hiring and clearance bottlenecks for government AI-security surge expertise.

nodes.name: GOLD EAGLE cybersecurity clearinghouse
nodes.jurisdiction: United States federal
nodes.description: Treasury and security partners coordinate AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and remediation.
nodes.mechanism: Deconflicts scanning and prioritizes patch information through voluntary industry collaboration.

powers.detail: Participants share vulnerability and response information.
Clearinghouse coordination is not a universal disclosure mandate.
Coordinates technical discovery and validation with participating organizations.
Coordinates mitigation with cooperating organisations. The clearinghouse does not itself acquire a general power to order model remedies.

gaps.detail: Success depends on participating labs, maintainers and operators sharing usable information.
Coordination does not replace sector regulators or criminal process.

nodes.name: International AI Safety Report
nodes.jurisdiction: International scientific assessment; location schematic, no regulatory jurisdiction
nodes.description: Independent synthesis of evidence about general-purpose AI capabilities, risks and risk management. It does not recommend particular policies.
nodes.mechanism: Scientific evidence for policymakers

powers.detail: Draws on research and expert contributions.
No compulsory disclosure powers.
Synthesises technical evidence; it is not an incident-investigation authority.
Does not impose remedies.

gaps.detail: The report describes scientific uncertainty and limits of pre-deployment testing.
Proprietary model evidence limits external scrutiny.

nodes.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
nodes.jurisdiction: US-based research; proposals may inform other jurisdictions
nodes.description: Provides a common structure for identifying and managing AI risks across an organisation.
nodes.mechanism: Risk management framework and generative AI profile

powers.detail: Adopting organisations gather information as part of their risk management.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.
Supports assessment practices; the document does not investigate companies.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.

gaps.detail: Voluntary guidance creates no general disclosure or deployment-control power.
A process framework is not evidence that a particular frontier model is safe.

nodes.name: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy
nodes.jurisdiction: US-based research; proposals may inform other jurisdictions
nodes.description: Develops policy proposals for internal model-use risk reporting and government AI surge capacity.
nodes.mechanism: Reporting design and preparedness research

powers.detail: Can solicit evidence from government, developers and researchers.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.
Analyses risk and governance; does not acquire an enforcement mandate.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.

gaps.detail: Its 2025 surge-capacity analysis identifies specialist hiring and mobilisation bottlenecks. This is an attributed diagnosis, not a current headcount audit.
Proposed reporting duties need adoption by a competent lawmaker or organisation.

nodes.name: Centre for Long-Term Resilience
nodes.jurisdiction: UK-based policy research; no public enforcement jurisdiction
nodes.description: Examines UK influence through AISI expertise, developer relationships and international convening.
nodes.mechanism: Policy advice on UK frontier governance

powers.detail: Can seek information and engage policymakers.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.
Policy analysis rather than compulsory technical inspection.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.

gaps.detail: Influence depends on relationships and information-sharing across institutions.
Recommended reforms do not themselves expand UK AISI powers.

nodes.name: Internal-use risk reporting proposal
nodes.jurisdiction: International voluntary standard; no sovereign jurisdiction
nodes.description: IAPS proposes reporting when materially more capable or risky models are used inside a developer. This proposal is separate from existing SB53 summaries.
nodes.mechanism: Structured assessment of autonomous behaviour and insider risks

powers.detail: Would collect internal-use evidence if adopted.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.
Helps reviewers reason about internal-use risk; not independent investigatory authority.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.

gaps.detail: A research proposal alone cannot compel reporting.
Internal systems and usage can be invisible to external evaluators.

nodes.name: AI surge-capacity proposals
nodes.jurisdiction: US-based research; proposals may inform other jurisdictions
nodes.status: Proposed; not a standing universal corps
nodes.description: Prearranged expert support could help government respond when specialist AI capacity is urgently needed.
nodes.mechanism: Proposed surge contracts and reserve expertise

powers.detail: Proposed arrangements require participating institutions and experts.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.
Additional experts could support investigations under the host authority’s remit.
No compulsory authority is created by this research or voluntary mechanism.

gaps.detail: Extra people must be recruited, cleared and available; a proposal is not operational readiness.
Experts still need relevant evidence and secure access.
A reserve corps would not itself create missing legal powers.

nodes.name: Mistral AI
nodes.jurisdiction: France / European Union; applicable destination-market laws
nodes.description: French model developer combining hosted products with downloadable model releases.
nodes.mechanism: Published usage restrictions, reporting and account enforcement for hosted products; moderation and configurable guardrail tools.

powers.detail: Can request internal information and receive reports about its products.
No sovereign power to compel disclosure by outside organizations.
Can review its own models and hosted-product evidence within its access.
Can change its own services and suspend accounts under applicable terms.

gaps.detail: Corporate enforcement is not regulatory authority over other developers.
Its usage policy expressly excludes open-source models and customer- or partner-hosted deployments; controls depend on deployment arrangements.

nodes.name: Hugging Face
nodes.jurisdiction: US company with global platform; applicable local laws and platform terms
nodes.description: Repository and distribution platform for models, datasets and applications, including releases from Mistral and Meta.
nodes.mechanism: Content reports and review, repository gating, removal or disabling, and account suspension under platform policy.

powers.detail: Can request cooperation or modifications from repository owners.
Platform terms do not confer public subpoena authority.
Can review hosted content and available platform evidence; complete model forensics may require further access.
Can remove or disable content it hosts and suspend accounts under its policy.

gaps.detail: Already-downloaded weights exist on independent systems; repository removal does not recall those copies (architectural inference from download documentation).
Control over a hosted repository does not confer authority over every downstream deployment.

nodes.name: Brazil National Data Protection Agency
nodes.jurisdiction: Brazil; personal-data processing within LGPD scope
nodes.description: ANPD applies personal-data law to AI training and use. Its existing privacy powers include obtaining records, inspecting systems and pursuing compliance or sanctions. This card does not treat Brazil's proposed general AI legislation as enacted.
nodes.mechanism: LGPD and ANPD inspection/sanctions procedure

powers.detail: May request relevant personal-data processing information.
Regulated parties must supply documents/data and a knowledgeable representative under article 5.
May access relevant systems, equipment and technical information and conduct or require audits, within privacy jurisdiction.
Can pursue compliance measures and LGPD sanctions through applicable procedures.

gaps.detail: A privacy violation provides a legal route; dangerous capabilities alone do not establish LGPD jurisdiction.
Statutory system access does not establish sufficient frontier-evaluation expertise; staffing is not assessed.

nodes.name: Technology Innovation Institute / Falcon
nodes.jurisdiction: United Arab Emirates; TII's own research, releases and systems
nodes.description: TII develops Falcon models and supports open-model collaboration through the Falcon Foundation. It is the applied-research pillar of Abu Dhabi's ATRC. The corporate layer here describes developer control, not private ownership.
nodes.mechanism: Internal research/release governance and open-model ecosystem

powers.detail: Institutional management can obtain internal development information.
No general power to compel information from external actors.
Can technically examine its own models and research systems.
Can change its own releases and systems; distributed copies are outside direct operational control.

gaps.detail: External investigation requires artifacts, cooperation or an applicable legal route.
Open distribution separates developer control from downstream deployment. The network edge is analytical, not a membership claim.

nodes.name: Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority
nodes.jurisdiction: Saudi Arabia; binding powers below concern personal-data law, including in-scope overseas processing
nodes.status: Operating; separate law and ethics roles
nodes.description: SDAIA combines data governance and AI policy. Its AI Ethics Principles guide responsible development; those principles alone do not establish coercive frontier-model powers. Binding powers below concern its personal-data oversight role and the PDPL's competent-authority procedures.
nodes.mechanism: PDPL oversight plus separate AI Ethics Principles

powers.detail: PDPL article 30 permits necessary controller documents and information.
Controllers must cooperate and make processing records available under articles 30–31; limited to PDPL scope.
Designated personnel inspect PDPL violations under article 37; this is not unrestricted frontier-model investigation.
PDPL committees can issue warnings/fines; cooperation and compliance obligations apply. The ethics principles alone create no general model-remedy order.

gaps.detail: Personal-data authority and AI ethical expectations have different legal bases; do not generalize one into universal frontier oversight.
Technical inspections, administrative committees and criminal prosecution have different roles.
